title: Design live comments
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, fan-out estimates, WebSocket gateways, sampling, batching, moderation.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Live comments are the scrolling chat beside a live stream or match: viewers post short messages and everyone watching sees them within a second or two. Think Twitch chat, YouTube Live chat, Instagram Live comments, Hotstar during an IPL match. The twist is the fan-out: one comment must reach millions of watchers.

Functional requirements

  • Post a comment on a live stream.
  • Every viewer of that stream sees new comments in near real time, in a sensible order.
  • Load recent history when joining (last 50 comments).
  • Moderation: delete a comment, block a user, rate limit, spam filter.
  • Optional: likes on comments, replay comments with the recorded video.

Non-functional requirements

  • End-to-end latency under 2 s p99.
  • Scale: 25M concurrent viewers on one stream (Hotstar reported 25M+ concurrent for cricket), 50k comments per second at a peak moment.
  • High availability; losing a few comments is acceptable, losing the whole chat is not (best-effort delivery).
  • Viewers cannot possibly read 50k comments/s, so sampling is allowed.

Decision gravity. Choose best-effort delivery with server-side sampling over guaranteed delivery of every comment. Exactly-once, ordered delivery to millions is extremely costly and nobody can read it anyway. It is reversible per stream (you can lower sampling for small streams).

Everyday analogy. A stadium announcer reading a few of the crowd's shouts over the loudspeaker; he cannot read all 50,000.

Common interview traps.

  • Promising guaranteed, ordered delivery of every comment to every viewer.
  • Using polling every second for 25M viewers (25M requests/s).
  • Treating a small chat room and a mega-stream as the same design.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Writes are plain HTTPS; reads are a persistent connection (WebSocket, SSE, or long-poll fallback).

POST /v1/streams/s_77/comments
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{ "text": "What a six!", "clientMsgId": "c_2f9a" }

201 { "commentId": "cm_01HF...", "createdAt": "2026-11-09T14:00:03.120Z" }
429 -> slow down (per-user rate limit)
403 -> user muted/blocked

clientMsgId makes retries idempotent (a retry does not post twice).

// Subscribe: WebSocket
GET wss://chat.example.com/v1/streams/s_77/subscribe?token=...&since=cm_01HF...
-> server frames (batched every 500 ms):
{ "type": "batch", "streamId": "s_77", "comments": [
    { "id":"cm_..", "user":"asha", "text":"What a six!", "ts": 1731160803120 } ],
  "dropped": 1840 }
GET /v1/streams/s_77/comments?limit=50&before=cm_01HF...
200 { "comments": [ ... ], "nextCursor": "..." }

DELETE /v1/streams/s_77/comments/cm_01HF...   (moderator)  -> 204

Server pushes a delete frame so viewers remove the comment from view. dropped tells clients that sampling occurred.

Industry example. Twitch chat is IRC over WebSocket; YouTube Live chat is polled/streamed in batches; Hotstar described pushing events over persistent connections with heavy batching.

Everyday analogy. A radio phone-in: callers speak one at a time into the studio, then the broadcast reaches everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • No since cursor, so reconnects lose or duplicate messages.
  • Sending one frame per comment instead of batching.
  • Letting viewers write directly to a socket without auth and rate limits.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume a mega-event: 25M concurrent viewers, 50k comments/s at peak, 100 bytes per comment.

Quantity Calculation Result
Connections 25M WebSockets; one box holds ~100k-500k idle conns (kernel tuned, ~10 KB each) ~100-250 gateway servers at 100k each
Naive fan-out 50k comments/s x 25M viewers 1.25 trillion deliveries/s: impossible
Sampled show ~20 comments/s per viewer (what a human reads) 25M x 20 = 500M msgs/s; still large
Batched one frame per 500 ms with 10 comments = ~1.2 KB 25M x 2 frames/s = 50M frames/s, ~60 GB/s = ~480 Gbit/s
Tiered gateway fan-out per box: 100k conns x 2 frames/s 200k frames/s per box: fine
Storage 50k/s x 100 B = 5 MB/s; if a 3 h match avg 10k/s 3 h x 3,600 x 10k x 100 B = ~11 GB per match
Memory per stream ring buffer of last 200 comments tiny (~20 KB)

Key insight: the problem is fan-out bandwidth, not storage. We reduce it by sampling (less content), batching (fewer packets), and a hierarchical broadcast tree (fewer hops from the source).

Industry example. Hotstar's 25M concurrent record in 2019 and the published trick of capping per-viewer message rate.

Everyday analogy. Newspapers print one edition, not 25 million personalised ones.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing storage but not egress.
  • Forgetting the cost per open connection (memory, file descriptors).
  • Assuming one machine can hold all the sockets.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components:

  • Comment service: validates, authenticates, rate-limits (Redis token bucket: 1 comment per 2 s per user), runs a fast spam/profanity filter, publishes to Kafka.
  • Kafka topic partitioned by streamId (hot streams get sub-partitions) preserves roughly ordered comments per stream.
  • Stream aggregator: reads a stream's partition, samples/batches (for example, the top 20 per 500 ms window, picked by recency, mentions or priority), writes one batch message to the pub/sub tier.
  • Pub/sub tier (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS or Kafka): a few channels per stream, each subscribed by gateways.
  • WebSocket gateways: each holds ~100k sockets, subscribed to the batch channels of the streams its users watch; fans out locally.
  • Comment store: Cassandra/DynamoDB keyed (streamId, timeBucket) for history and replay; Redis ring buffer for the last 50 on join.
  • Moderation service: async classifier, deletion events flow through the same channel.

Decision gravity: push via persistent connections vs polling. Push: 25M sockets, low latency. Polling: simple and CDN-friendly but 25M requests/s unless polling every 5 s with CDN-cached batches (2 s TTL). YouTube Live chat and Facebook Live use batched cached responses effectively for huge streams. Switching modes is reversible per client version, but scaling the gateway tier is expensive; start with polling-on-CDN for mega streams if latency of 3-5 s is tolerable.

Decision gravity: sampling server-side. Why: bounded per-viewer bandwidth. Alternative: send everything and let the client drop (wastes egress). Breaks when users feel their comment never appears: always show a user their own comment locally (optimistic echo). Reversible.

Industry examples. Twitch (IRC-based chat clusters), Facebook Live (batched polling plus long-lived connections), Hotstar (fan-out tree), Slack/Discord (gateway shards, guild-level routing).

Everyday analogy. A radio network: one studio, regional transmitters, and each listener's receiver does the last mile.

Common interview traps.

  • A single Redis pub/sub channel for 25M viewers.
  • Skipping the aggregator and hammering gateways with 50k messages/s.
  • No story for deletes/moderation.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Fan-out tree and batching

One batch per 500 ms per stream goes to a handful of relays; each relay forwards to its gateways; each gateway writes the same bytes to its 100k sockets. Serialising once and sharing the buffer (zero-copy) keeps CPU low. Decision: 500 ms windows trade 0.5 s extra latency for 10-20x fewer frames. Reversible by configuration.

Connection tier

Tune the OS: ulimit -n 1000000, net.core.somaxconn=65535, net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, per-connection buffers small (4 KB). Use an event-loop stack (Netty, Go, Erlang/Elixir; WhatsApp's Erlang servers famously held about 2M connections per box in a published benchmark). Heartbeat every 30 s; drop dead sockets. Load balance by L4 with least connections, and use connection draining on deploy with jittered reconnects to avoid a reconnect storm.

Ordering and ids

Comment ids are time-sortable (ULID or Snowflake: timestamp + shard + sequence), so a since cursor works. Strict global order across partitions is unnecessary; order by id within a batch. Decision: per-stream ordering via a single partition owner is simpler but a hot spot; hot streams get multiple partitions and merge by timestamp in the aggregator.

Storage and replay

Cassandra partition key (streamId, minuteBucket) keeps partitions bounded (50k/s x 60 = 3M rows per minute for the mega stream; split with a hash suffix bucket = hash(commentId) % 8). TTL 30 days unless saved for replay. Late joiners read the ring buffer from Redis (O(1)), never Cassandra.

Moderation and abuse

Rate limit per user and per IP (token bucket), shadow-banning (the author sees their comment, others do not), blocklists in memory with a Bloom filter or Aho-Corasick, ML toxicity model async with delete event on hit. Verified/subscriber badges raise priority in sampling. Decision: fast sync filter + slow async model keeps latency low while catching more.

Choosing which comments to show

Score = recency + author priority (moderator, creator, subscriber) + mentions + engagement; pick top K per window. Dedupe repeated spam ("GG GG GG") with a short-window hash counter.

Failure and degradation

Gateway down: clients reconnect with since id and get missed batches from the ring buffer. Pub/sub loss is tolerated; chat is lossy by design. Overload: drop to lower sampling ratio first, then stop accepting new comments before stopping reads (reading is the product).

Production incident patterns. (1) Reconnect storm after deploy pins CPU on gateways: metric is connection accept rate; add jitter and drain slowly. (2) One hot partition for the mega stream: Kafka lag on one broker; fix with sub-partitioning. (3) A raid of bots: surge in comments from new accounts; rate-limit by account age.

Industry examples. Twitch, Hotstar, Facebook Live, Discord's gateways.

Everyday analogy. A talk-radio host screens callers (moderation), reads a few (sampling) and the transmitter does the rest.

Common interview traps.

  • Strong ordering and exactly-once guarantees nobody needs.
  • Forgetting reconnect jitter.
  • Reading history from the primary DB on every join.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Recognising fan-out as the core problem and doing the 25M x rate arithmetic.
  • Sampling, batching and a broadcast tree to cut bandwidth.
  • Realistic WebSocket gateway sizing and OS tuning.
  • Best-effort semantics stated explicitly, with an optimistic echo for the author.
  • A separate storage path for history and replay.
  • Moderation, rate limits, and graceful degradation.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Fan-out dominates: 50k comments/s to 25M viewers is impossible naively.
  • Sample on the server, batch per 500 ms, and send through a tree of aggregators, relays and gateways.
  • Kafka per stream for ingestion, Redis ring buffer for join history, Cassandra for durable storage.
  • Gateways hold ~100k sockets each; reconnect with jitter and a since cursor.
  • Best-effort delivery and per-window ordering are enough.
  • Moderation: sync rate limit and filters, async ML, delete events pushed to clients.
  • Degrade by lowering sampling, then rejecting writes, never the reads.

questions.subtopic: Delivery semantics and push vs poll
questions.promptHtml: For live comments on a stream with millions of viewers, should delivery be guaranteed and ordered? How should viewers receive new comments: push or polling?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you pick a semantic that fits the product, and whether you see fan-out as the core problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Best-effort. No viewer can read 50,000 comments a second, so guaranteed, ordered delivery of every comment to every viewer is extremely costly and useless. I'd sample on the server, batch, and tolerate a few lost comments, but never lose the whole chat. For receiving, naive polling every second from 25M viewers is 25M requests/s. I'd push over WebSockets (or SSE), or for the very biggest streams use polling of CDN-cached batches (2 s TTL) if a latency of 3-5 s is acceptable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Commenter -> Comment API -> Chat service -> Fan-out -> Viewers
                              |
                         Comment store (history/replay)
  • Requirements: end-to-end latency under 2 s p99; 25M concurrent viewers; 50k comments/s at a peak moment.
  • Naive fan-out: 50k x 25M = 1.25 trillion deliveries per second. Impossible; so reduce content (sampling), packets (batching) and hops (broadcast tree).
  • Always show a user their own comment locally (optimistic echo), so sampling doesn't make them feel ignored.
  • A small chat room and a mega-stream are different designs; use thresholds per stream.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Promising exactly-once, ordered delivery to millions.
  • Polling every second at this scale.
  • Using one design for tiny and huge streams.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you lose with best-effort? -> Some comments are dropped for some viewers; the dropped counter in a frame tells clients sampling occurred.
  2. What about history? -> A Redis ring buffer of the last 50 on join; Cassandra for replay.
  3. Is polling ever right? -> Yes, with CDN-cached batches for mega streams where 3-5 s latency is fine.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer proposes WebSockets and a database. The senior answer names best-effort semantics explicitly and shows the arithmetic that forces sampling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that tried to deliver every message in order to every viewer ran out of gateway bandwidth within minutes of a big match.

questions.contextHtml: Mega-event: 25M concurrent viewers, 50k comments/s at peak, 100 bytes per comment. A gateway box holds about 100k connections (a figure to verify with a load test). The product owner says "just send everything to everyone".
questions.promptHtml: Show why that fails and size a workable design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Computes only storage (5 MB/s, tiny) and concludes it's easy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many comments per second can a viewer meaningfully read (about 20)? Is 500 ms batching acceptable? Is it fine if some comments aren't shown to everyone?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (planning).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The cost is egress and per-connection overhead, not storage.
  4. How I'd verify each: Connections: 25M / 100k = 250 gateways. Naive: 50k x 25M = 1.25 trillion deliveries per second (impossible). Sampled to 20 msgs/s per viewer: 25M x 20 = 500M messages/s, still large. Batched: one frame per 500 ms carrying about 10 comments (about 1.2 KB) means 25M x 2 frames/s = 50M frames/s, about 60 GB/s = about 480 Gbit/s. Per gateway: 100k connections x 2 frames/s = 200k frames/s, which is fine. Storage: a 3 h match averaging 10k/s is 3 x 3,600 x 10,000 x 100 B = about 11 GB.
  5. Root cause: n/a. Fan-out multiplies one input by 25M.
  6. Fix: Server-side sampling, 500 ms batching, a broadcast tree (aggregator, regional relays, gateways), serialise once and share the buffer.
  7. Prevention: Per-gateway frame rate, egress and connection count metrics; load test at full connection count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not let clients drop messages after receiving them (wastes egress). I would not reduce batching window below what latency needs, since frames per second rise.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the viewer count is 100M? -> More gateways, regional relays and lower sampling per viewer; the tree depth grows slowly.
  • How about reducing the 480 Gbit/s? -> Compress, shrink fields, lower comments per frame.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch plan sized the storage tier carefully and forgot egress; the first big stream saturated the gateways' uplinks in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Storage-only math.
  • Hire: Shows 25M x rate, sampling/batching effect and gateway count.
  • Strong hire: Egress in Gbit/s, per-gateway frame rate, explicit assumptions.

questions.promptHtml: Where in the pipeline do you sample and batch comments, how do you choose which ones to show, and how do you order them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you can place the reduction at the right layer and reason about ordering without demanding global order.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A stream aggregator reads that stream's Kafka partition and, per 500 ms window, picks the top K comments by a score: recency, author priority (moderator, creator, subscriber), mentions and engagement, after de-duplicating spam like repeated "GG GG GG". It writes one batch to the pub/sub tier, and gateways fan the same bytes out to their sockets. Order is by time-sortable id (ULID or Snowflake) within a batch; strict global order across partitions isn't needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kafka (per stream) -> Stream aggregator (sample + batch) -> Pub/sub shards -> Gateways -> Viewers
  • Sampling server-side bounds per-viewer bandwidth. Doing it on the client wastes egress.
  • 500 ms windows trade 0.5 s extra latency for 10-20x fewer frames.
  • Kafka is partitioned by streamId; hot streams get sub-partitions that the aggregator merges by timestamp.
  • Ids embed a timestamp, so since=<id> cursors work on reconnect.
  • Optimistic echo: show the author's comment immediately, regardless of sampling.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping the aggregator and hammering gateways with 50k messages/s.
  • A single Redis pub/sub channel for 25M viewers.
  • Sampling with no way for users to see their own comment.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the aggregator dies? -> Stand-by consumer takes over the partition; viewers see a short gap, which is acceptable.
  2. How do you stop spam from winning? -> Dedupe by short-window hash counters and rate limits per user.
  3. Why not a single owner per stream for strict order? -> Simple but a hot spot; merge by timestamp from multiple partitions instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "publish to a channel". The senior answer places sampling in an aggregator, picks scoring features and justifies weak ordering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team without an aggregator saw gateways melt at a goal moment, when comment rate spiked 10x.

questions.contextHtml:
You deploy a new gateway version during a live match, restarting 250 gateways in two waves. Metrics:

14:02:10 gateways restarted
14:02:12 connection accepts/s: 8k -> 410k      gateway cpu: 35% -> 98%
14:02:20 tls handshake failures 22%            LB 5xx 14%
14:02:40 clients retrying every 1 s with no backoff; connected users 25M -> 6M

ulimit -n and kernel settings were verified earlier this week.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you stabilise and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more gateways" while the clients keep retrying every second, or blaming kernel tuning (a red herring).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do clients use jitter and backoff? Was connection draining used? How many users were connected before? Did the restart waves overlap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the rollout, shed load at the LB (return 503 with Retry-After for new connections beyond a rate), let gateways recover by admitting connections gradually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Synchronised reconnect: 25M clients reconnect at once after restarts. (b) TLS handshakes are CPU heavy, so CPU saturates. (c) No backoff makes it a retry storm. Kernel limits were checked, so unlikely.
  4. How I'd verify each: Accept-rate graphs aligned with the restart time; client logs showing fixed 1 s retry; CPU profile (handshake time).
  5. Root cause: Mass simultaneous reconnect without jitter or backoff.
  6. Fix: Short-term: throttle accepts, restore gradually. Long-term: clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus random jitter (for instance 0-30 s), connection draining on deploy (slowly close and shift connections), rolling deploys in small batches, TLS session resumption, resume via since cursor so no data is refetched in bulk.
  7. Prevention: Deploy canary with a small wave first, a max-accept-rate limit at the LB, an alert on accept rate, chaos tests for gateway restarts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Jitter of up to 30 s delays some viewers but protects everyone. I would not restart the remaining gateways to "fix" it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you hold the CPU cost of handshakes? -> Session tickets and TLS offload at an L4/L7 tier.
  • What if all old clients have no jitter? -> Server-side: send a randomised "reconnect after N s" on graceful close.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A deploy mid-match turned 25M viewers into a self-inflicted DDoS. The next quarter's rule: gateway rollouts drain at a fixed percent per minute with a server-suggested reconnect delay.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds capacity.
  • Hire: Finds synchronised reconnect, adds jitter/backoff and drain.
  • Strong hire: Server-driven retry hints, canary, accept-rate limits and handshake costs.

questions.contextHtml:
User reports: some comments appear twice, others vanish after their phone switched from Wi-Fi to 4G. Client code (simplified):

POST /v1/streams/s_77/comments   { "text": "What a six!" }      // no clientMsgId
on timeout -> retry the POST up to 3 times
on socket close -> reconnect to wss://chat.example.com/v1/streams/s_77/subscribe?token=...   // no since

Server log: comment cm_01HF1 and cm_01HF2 text="What a six!" user=asha created 1.1 s apart.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix the API contract.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce the timeout" or "dedupe by text on the client".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the first POST succeed server-side when the client sees a timeout? How long should the server remember client ids? What gap size is acceptable on reconnect?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side short-window duplicate suppression (same user, same text, within a couple of seconds) while the client fix ships.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Retry of a non-idempotent POST creates a duplicate when the first request succeeded but the response was lost. (b) Reconnect without since loses messages sent during the gap (or replays arbitrary ones).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log pairs with the same user and text a retry-interval apart; client logs for reconnect timing; compare ids around the gap.
  5. Root cause: No idempotency key on writes and no resume cursor on reads.
  6. Fix: Client generates clientMsgId (for example c_2f9a) per comment; server stores (userId, clientMsgId) for a few minutes and returns the same commentId on retry. On reconnect send since=<last comment id>; the server replays missed batches from the Redis ring buffer. Ids are time-sortable (ULID/Snowflake), so cursors work. Return dropped counts so the client knows sampling happened.
  7. Prevention: Contract tests for retries (kill the connection after the server commits), alert on duplicate rate, ring buffer size sized for the longest reconnect gap.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Chat is lossy by design, so I don't need exactly-once for reads, just a bounded replay. I would not dedupe by text; users legitimately repeat messages.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the gap is longer than the ring buffer? -> Fetch the recent 50 from history and continue; show a "some comments skipped" hint.
  • How long to keep idempotency keys? -> Longer than the client's retry window (minutes).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching networks on mobile caused the retry bug to appear only in the field, never in the office. The idempotency key fixed duplicates without server-side text matching.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Client-side text dedupe.
  • Hire: clientMsgId and since cursor.
  • Strong hire: Notes lossy semantics, ring buffer sizing, contract tests.

questions.contextHtml:
During the final over, one Kafka partition is behind:

topic comments  partitions 48  keyed by streamId
partition 31 (stream s_77): lag 2.4M   msg/s in: 52k   consumer: 1 aggregator at 100% cpu
other partitions: lag 0, msg/s 300-1,500
end-to-end latency for s_77: 1.4 s -> 38 s       Cassandra writer for (s_77, minute) hot, timeouts 6%
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without breaking ordering semantics.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add partitions" (this doesn't move an existing key's traffic) or "add consumers" (a partition has one consumer in a group).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is strict ordering required for this stream? Can the aggregator merge multiple partitions? What is the Cassandra partition key?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise sampling (drop more low-priority comments at the comment service before Kafka), shed writes to history to a lower priority, and increase aggregator CPU/instance size if possible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) All traffic for one stream goes to one partition and one consumer: a hot key. (b) The aggregator does sampling and batching in a single thread. (c) Cassandra partition (streamId, minuteBucket) is too hot: 52k/s x 60 = about 3M rows per minute in one partition.
  4. How I'd verify each: Consumer group lag per partition, CPU per consumer thread, Cassandra partition size and write latency.
  5. Root cause: A single-key partitioning model meets a mega-stream.
  6. Fix: Sub-partition hot streams: key by streamId + (hash(commentId) % N) so the stream spreads across N partitions and the aggregator merges by timestamp/id; aggregators consume the N partitions. For storage use (streamId, minuteBucket, hash(commentId) % 8). Do the sampling earlier (at the comment service) when rate is above a threshold.
  7. Prevention: Per-partition lag alert, automatic N for streams by rate, load test with a mega-stream.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Strict per-stream order via one partition is simpler but is the bottleneck; weak order merged by id is fine for chat. I would not add consumers to the same partition expecting parallelism.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about order across sub-partitions? -> Merge by ULID/timestamp inside a batch; small skew is invisible.
  • Rebalancing during the event? -> Avoid; change the key at stream start for known big events.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cup final produced a single hot partition that no one expected, because all previous load tests used many mid-size streams. Sub-partitioning was added the next day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add partitions/consumers blindly.
  • Hire: Hot key analysis, sub-partitions with merge.
  • Strong hire: Storage bucket split, earlier sampling, per-stream auto N.

questions.contextHtml: For a one-off 25M-viewer stream the infra team estimates 250 WebSocket gateways plus a relay tree. A product engineer suggests: "Let clients poll /comments?since= every 3 seconds, and let the CDN cache the response with a 2 s TTL." Latency requirement: comments visible within about 2 s p99, but a stakeholder says 4-5 s would be acceptable for this event only. Infra budget is tight and the team has never operated that many sockets.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and what is the decision gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "WebSockets because it's real time" or "polling because it's simple", without numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 4-5 s acceptable and is it written down? Is this a recurring product or one event? Will users post from the same page (need a write path anyway)? CDN capacity and cost per request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Polling every 3 s from 25M is about 8.3M requests/s, but identical responses for ?since= cursors that align on batch boundaries are cacheable, so the CDN absorbs it and the origin sees a trickle. WebSockets give lower latency and lower per-viewer request overhead but need 250+ gateways, connection tuning and reconnect-storm discipline.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype the cached batch endpoint and measure CDN hit ratio and cost; load test a gateway at 100k sockets; compare the latency budget.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The deciding variable is the latency requirement and operating experience.
  6. Fix: For this event use cached batch polling (cache key = stream + batch sequence, 2 s TTL), with the write path on plain HTTPS. Keep the message format (batches with ids) identical so it can move to WebSockets later. For recurring, latency-critical products invest in the gateway tier.
  7. Prevention: Test cache hit ratio per batch key, protect the origin with request collapsing, clock-align batches so clients converge on the same keys.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Switching modes is reversible per client version, but scaling the gateway tier is expensive, so I start with the cheaper option when the requirement allows. I would not use polling for a feature that needs sub-second chat.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the stakeholder now wants 1 s latency? -> Move to WebSockets or SSE; the batch format survives.
  • Cache stampede at batch expiry? -> Collapsing and a per-batch immutable key (sequence number) rather than a TTL on a moving URL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked polling-on-CDN for a big event, hit 97% CDN hit ratio and avoided building a socket fleet it would use once.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks by buzzword.
  • Hire: Does the request math and links choice to the latency requirement.
  • Strong hire: Immutable batch keys, same payload format for later migration, reversibility reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
During a streamer's launch, a raid posted abusive spam. Timeline:

20:00 new accounts (< 1 h old) comments/s: 40 -> 9,500    spam share of sampled comments: 63%
20:03 sync keyword filter catches 18%     async ML classifier lag: 7 min
20:05 moderators delete 4,000 comments; deletes reach viewers after 45-90 s
20:07 legit viewers complain they see only spam; creator's own comments often not displayed
questions.promptHtml: Write the review: what failed and which controls do you add?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hire more moderators" or "turn on a bigger ML model".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How did the accounts get created (a signup wave)? Why did the sampler favour spam (scoring, duplicate handling)? Why did deletes take 45-90 s (batch pipeline versus a push path)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Slow mode and follower-only or subscriber-only chat; rate-limit by account age; raise sampling priority for the creator, moderators and subscribers; shadow-ban flagged accounts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Sampling scored recency and volume and had no dedupe; new accounts had the same limits as old ones; ML ran asynchronously and was too slow; delete events went through the same batched path as comments with a long window.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare account age distribution against the baseline; sampler score features; the delete event latency from moderator action to client frame.
  5. Root cause: Defences were layered but not fast: weak sync filter, slow async model, rate limits not tied to account age, and slow deletion propagation.
  6. Fix: Token-bucket limits by user, IP and account age (brand-new accounts get a very low rate); dedupe repeated text with a short-window hash counter; sampling priority for creator, moderators, subscribers and verified; a fast sync filter (blocklist via Bloom filter or Aho-Corasick) plus the async ML toxicity model emitting delete events; delete frames pushed immediately on a priority channel (not waiting for the next batch); shadow-banning (author sees their comment, others don't).
  7. Prevention: Alert on comments/s from accounts younger than X, spam ratio, delete propagation latency; drills with synthetic raids; a clear runbook (slow mode, followers-only).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Stricter limits on new accounts hurt some genuine new users; I accept that during a raid and relax automatically. I would not block all comments; reading is the product, so degrade by lowering sampling first and rejecting new writes before reads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you avoid false positives from the ML model? -> Send borderline items to a review queue instead of hard delete.
  • Can the sync filter be bypassed with spelling tricks? -> Yes; normalise text and rely on the async model as a second layer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A raid succeeded not because filters were absent but because deletes took a minute to reach viewers. Putting deletes on a priority channel changed the experience more than a better model.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More moderators or a bigger model.
  • Hire: Account-age limits, dedupe, priority sampling, fast delete path.
  • Strong hire: Layered sync plus async design, runbook, metrics and degradation order.
